newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end higher but downtrend intact.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end higher but downtrend intact.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended slightly higher Tuesday, helped by some fund shortcovering, but the downtrend of the past month remains intact, traders said.
"Sentiment is still bearish," Credit Suisse New York-based vice president Ian MacDonald said.

"The IMF postponed a decision on gold sales this week, but there is a feeling central bank activity remains a cloud over the market, while physical demand from industry is not picking up in line with usual seasonal patterns and U.S. dollar strength is not helping either," he said.
"Having said that, in the last three and a half years, whenever gold has got down into the $370-380 area, it has not stayed there very long," he said.
COMEX December gold ended up 50 cents at $381.00 an ounce, after trading in a $379.00-381.50 range.

In New York bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted around $378.60 an ounce, compared with the London afternoon fix at $378.65, and up from the morning fix at $377.05, which was the lowest since March 6, 1995.
COMEX December silver ended up 3.30 cents at $4.910 an ounce, after trading in a $4.850-4.955 range.
Earlier COMEX announced Wilmington Trust in Delaware held silver stocks in deliverable form of 59.4 million ounces as of September 30, less than many analysts expected.
Wilmington Trust is due to become an official exchange depositary on January 1, 1997.

NYMEX October platinum ended down 10 cents at $384.30 an ounce, after trading up to $386.00 intraday, and back months ended higher, helped by news the U.S. government's fiscal 1997 appropriations bill, which passed Monday, had included the planned authority for the U.S. Mint to issue platinum coins next year.
The U.S. Mint could call on U.S. government stocks of platinum as working inventory but these stocks would need to be replaced, providing some extra demand for platinum, analysts said.
NYMEX December palladium ended up 75 cents at $120.50 an ounce.

Precious metals have been in a month long downtrend, led by fund selling. Investor demand is limited by low inflation and a strong equity market, while industrial and investor demand in other countries has been restrained by a strong U.S. dollar pushing up the cost of precious metals in local currencies, analysts said.
